entries.158caad88060694a98bac2dc0c0609f203f7cef2: <div sID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="2Kgs.14" sID="2Kgs.14"/> <div eID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7383" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues the history of the succession in the kingdoms both of Judah and Israel. I. In the kingdom of Judah here is, 1. The entire history (as much as is recorded in this book) of Amaziah's reign (1.) His good character, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. (2.) The justice he executed on the murderers of his father, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.5-2Kgs.14.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. (3.) His victory over the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">ver. 7</reference>. (4.) His war with Joash, and his defeat in that war, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8-2Kgs.14.14">ver. 8-14</reference>. (5.) His fall, at last, by a conspiracy against him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.17-2Kgs.14.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. 2. The beginning of the history of Azariah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.21-2Kgs.14.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. II. In the kingdom of Israel, the conclusion of the reign of Joash (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>), and the entire history of Jeroboam his son, the second of that name, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.23-2Kgs.14.29">ver. 23-29</reference>. How many great men are made to stand in a little compass in God's book!
entries.8402068e1e747bf4914139de63744b9cecfc80bc: <div eID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7383" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reign of Amaziah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 828.)</title> <div sID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the second year of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel reigned Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah. <hi type="super">2</hi> He was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , yet not like David his father: he did according to all things as Joash his father did. <hi type="super">4</hi> Howbeit the high places were not taken away: as yet the people did sacrifice and burnt incense on the high places. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it came to pass, as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, that he slew his servants which had slain the king his father. <hi type="super">6</hi> But the children of the murderers he slew not: according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses, wherein the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded, saying, The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall be put to death for his own sin. <hi type="super">7</hi> He slew of Edom in the valley of salt ten thousand, and took Selah by war, and called the name of it Joktheel unto this day. <div eID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> Amaziah, the son and successor of Joash, is the king whom here we have an account of. Let us take a view of him, <div eID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> I. In the temple; and there he acted, in some measure, well, like Joash, but not like David, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.3">v. 3</reference>. He began well, but did not persevere: He <hi type="italic">did that which was right in the sight of the Lord,</hi> kept up his attendance on God's altars and his attention to God's word, yet not like David. It is not enough to do that which our pious predecessors did, merely to keep up the usage, but we must do it <hi type="italic">as</hi> they did it, from the same principle of faith and devotion and with the same sincerity and resolution. It is here taken notice of, as before, that <hi type="italic">the high places were not taken away,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.4">v. 4</reference>. It is hard to get clear of those corruptions which, by long usage, have gained both prescription and a favourable opinion. <div eID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> II. On the bench; and there we have him doing justice on the traitors that murdered his father, not as soon as ever he came to the crown, lest it should occasion some disturbance, but he prudently deferred it till <hi type="italic">the kingdom was confirmed in his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.5">v. 5</reference>. To weaken a factious party gradually, when it is not safe to provoke, often proves the way to ruin it effectually. Justice strikes surely by striking slowly, and is often executed most prudently when it is not executed presently. Wisdom here is profitable to direct. Amaziah did thus, 1. According to the rule of the law, that ancient rule, that <hi type="italic">he that sheds man's blood by man shall his blood be shed.</hi> Never let traitors or murderers expect to come to their graves like other men. <hi type="italic">Let them flee to the pit, and let no man stay them.</hi> 2. Under the limitation of the law: <hi type="italic">The children of the murderers he slew not,</hi> because the law of Moses had expressly provided that <hi type="italic">the children should not be put to death for the fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.6">v. 6</reference>. It is probable that this is taken notice of because there were those about him that advised him to that rigour, both in revenge (because the crime was extraordinary—the murder of a king) and in policy, that the children might not plot against him, in revenge of their father's death. But against these insinuations he opposed the express law of God (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.16">Deut. xxiv. 16</reference>), which he was to judge by, and which he resolved to adhere to and trust God with the issue. God visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, because every man is guilty before him and owes him a death; so that, if he require the life for the father's sin, he does not wrong, the sinner having forfeited it already by his own. But he does not allow earthly princes to do thus: the children, before them, are innocent, and therefore must not suffer as guilty. <div eID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> III. In the field; and there we find him triumphing over the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">v. 7</reference>. Edom had <hi type="italic">revolted from under the hand of Judah</hi> in Joram's time, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.22">ch. viii. 22</reference>. Now he makes war upon them to bring them back to their allegiance, kills 10,000 and takes the chief city of Arabia the stony (called <hi type="italic">Selah</hi>—<hi type="italic">a rock</hi>), and gave it a new name. We shall find a larger account of this expedition, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5-2Chr.25.13">2 Chron. xxv. 5</reference>, &c.
entries.b2c6a60127fdfd8336779cc14585621003c1fb6b: <div eID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash, the son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, Come, let us look one another in the face. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon sent to the cedar that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou hast indeed smitten Edom, and thine heart hath lifted thee up: glory <hi type="italic">of this,</hi> and tarry at home: for why shouldest thou meddle to <hi type="italic">thy</hi> hurt, that thou shouldest fall, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou, and Judah with thee? <hi type="super">11</hi> But Amaziah would not hear. Therefore Jehoash king of Israel went up; and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth-shemesh, which <hi type="italic">belongeth</hi> to Judah. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Judah was put to the worse before Israel; and they fled every man to their tents. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash the son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem, and brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate, four hundred cubits. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and in the treasures of the king's house, and hostages, and returned to Samaria. <div eID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> For several successions after the division of the kingdoms that of Judah suffered much by the <hi type="italic">enmity</hi> of Israel. After Asa's time, for several successions, it suffered more by the <hi type="italic">friendship</hi> of Israel, and by the alliance and affinity made with them. But now we meet with hostility between them again, which had not been for some ages before. <div eID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> I. Amaziah, upon no provocation, and without showing any cause of quarrel, challenged Joash into the field (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, let us look one another in the face;</hi> let us try our strength in battle." Had he challenged him to a personal duel only, the error would have remained with himself, but each must bring all their forces into the field, and thousands of lives on both sides must be sacrificed to his capricious humour. Hereby he showed himself proud, presumptuous, and prodigal of blood. Some think that he intended to avenge the injury which the dismissed disgusted Israelites had lately done to his country, in their return (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2 Chron. xxv. 13</reference>), and that he had also the vanity to think of subduing the kingdom of Israel, and reuniting it to Judah. A <hi type="italic">fool's lips thus enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes.</hi> Those that challenge are chargeable with that beginning of strife, which is as the letting forth of water. He that is eager either to fight or to go to law may perhaps have enough of it quickly, and be the first that repents it. <div eID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> II. Joash sent him a grave rebuke for his challenge, with advice to withdraw it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.9-2Kgs.14.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. 1. He mortifies his pride, by comparing himself to a cedar, a stately tree, and Amaziah to a thistle, a sorry weed, telling him he was so far from fearing him that he despised him, and scorned as much to have any thing to do with him, or make any alliance with him, as the cedar would to match his daughter to a thistle. The ancient house of David he thinks not worthy to be named the same day with the house of Jehu, though an upstart. How may a humble man smile to hear two proud and scornful men set their wits on work to vilify and undervalue one another! 2. He foretels his fall: <hi type="italic">A wild beast trode down the thistle,</hi> and so put an end to his treaty with the cedar; so easily does Joash think his forces can crush Amaziah, and so unable does he think him to make any resistance. 3. He shows him the folly of his challenge: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast indeed smitten Edom,</hi> a weak, unarmed, undisciplined body of men, and therefore thinkest thou canst carry all before thee and subdue the regular forces of Israel with as much ease. <hi type="italic">Thy heart has lifted thee up.</hi>" See where the root of all sin lies; it is in the heart, thence it flows, and that must bear the blame. It is not Providence, the event, the occasion (whatever it is), that makes men proud, or secure, or discontented, or the like, but it is their own heart that does it. "Thou art proud of the blow thou hast given to Edom, as if that had made thee formidable to all mankind." Those wretchedly deceive themselves that magnify their own performances, and, because they have been blessed with some little success and reputation, conclude themselves fit for any thing and no less sure of it. 4. He counsels him to be content with the honour he has won, and not to hazard that, by grasping at more that was out of his reach: <hi type="italic">Why shouldst thou meddle to thy hurt,</hi> as fools often do, that will be meddling? <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Prov. xx. 3</reference>. Many would have had wealth and honour enough if they had but known when they had enough. He warns him of the consequence, that it would be fatal not to himself only, but to his kingdom, which he ought to protect. <div eID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> III. Amaziah persisted in his resolution, and the issue was bad; he had better have tarried at home, for Joash gave him such a look in the face as put him to confusion. Challengers commonly prove to be on the losing side. 1. His army was routed and dispersed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.12">v. 12</reference>. Josephus says, When they were to engage they were struck with such terror that they did not strike a stroke, but every one made the best of his way. 2. He himself was taken prisoner by the king of Israel, and then had enough of <hi type="italic">looking him in the face.</hi> Amaziah's pedigree comes in here somewhat abruptly (<hi type="italic">the son of Joash, the son of Ahaziah</hi>), because perhaps he had gloried in the dignity of his ancestors, or because he now smarted for their iniquity. 3. The conqueror entered Jerusalem, which tamely opened to him, and yet he broke down their wall (and, as Josephus says, drove his chariot in triumph through the breach), in reproach to them, and that he might, when he pleased, take possession of the royal city. 4. He plundered Jerusalem, took away all that was valuable, and returned to Samaria, laden with spoils, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.14">v. 14</reference>. It was said of Joash that he did that which was <hi type="italic">evil in the sight of the Lord,</hi> and of Amaziah that he did <hi type="italic">that which was right;</hi> and yet Joash triumphs thus over Amaziah, and why so? Because God would show, in Amaziah's fate, that he resists the proud, or because, whatever they were otherwise, Joash had lately been respectful to one of God's prophets (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.14">ch. xiii. 14</reference>), but Amaziah had been abusive to another (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2 Chron. xxv. 16</reference>), and God will honour those who honour him in his prophets, but those who despise them, and him in them, shall be lightly esteemed.
entries.59eca4292505694bf8b04fd6d111c5e9f95ee5e4: <div eID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reign of Jeroboam, King of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 825.)</title> <div sID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash which he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? <hi type="super">16</hi> And Jehoash slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel; and Jeroboam his son reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel fifteen years. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the rest of the acts of Amaziah, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? <hi type="super">19</hi> Now they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem: and he fled to Lachish; but they sent after him to Lachish, and slew him there. <hi type="super">20</hi> And they brought him on horses: and he was buried at Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David. <hi type="super">21</hi> And all the people of Judah took Azariah, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah. <hi type="super">22</hi> He built Elath, and restored it to Judah, after that the king slept with his fathers. <div eID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7396" type="x-p"/> Here are three kings brought to their graves in these few verses:—1. Joash king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. We attended his funeral once before, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.12-2Kgs.13.13">ch. xiii. 12, 13</reference>. But, because the historian had occasion to give a further account of his life and actions, he again mentions his death and burial. 2. Amaziah king of Judah. Fifteen years he survived his conqueror the king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.17">v. 17</reference>. A man may live a great while after he has been shamed, may be thoroughly mortified (as Amaziah no doubt was) and yet not dead. His acts are said to be found written in his annals (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.18">v. 18</reference>), but not his might; for his cruelty when he was a conqueror over the Edomites, and his insolence when he challenged the king of Israel, showed him void of true courage. He was slain by his own subjects, who hated him for his maladministration (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.19">v. 19</reference>) and made Jerusalem too hot for him, the ignominious breach made in their walls being occasioned by his folly and presumption. He fled to Lachish. How long he continued concealed or sheltered there we are not told, but, at last, he was there murdered, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.19">v. 19</reference>. No further did the rage of the rebels extend, for they brought him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him there among his ancestors. 3. Azariah succeeded Amaziah, but not till twelve years after his father's death, for Amaziah died in the fifteenth year of Jeroboam (as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.23 2Kgs.13.2">v. 23 with v. 2</reference>), but Azariah did not begin his reign till the twenty-seventh of Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.1">ch. xv. 1</reference>), for he was but four years old at the death of his father, so that, for twelve years, till he came to be sixteen, the government was in the hands of protectors. He reigned very long (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.2">ch. xv. 2</reference>) and yet the account of his reign is here industriously huddled up, and broken off abruptly (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He built Elath</hi> (which had belonged to the Edomites, but, it is probable, was recovered by his father, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">after that the king slept with his fathers,</hi> as if that had been all he did that was worth mentioning, or rather it is meant of king Amaziah: he built it soon after Amaziah died.
entries.3cddbd007d14d997f1f8ce17cb15f6332cadd32f: <div eID="gen7396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7397" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria, <hi type="italic">and reigned</hi> forty and one years. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. <hi type="super">25</hi> He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> of Gath-hepher. <hi type="super">26</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saw the affliction of Israel, <hi type="italic">that it was</hi> very bitter: for <hi type="italic">there was</hi> not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven: but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash. <hi type="super">28</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, and all that he did, and his might, how he warred, and how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, <hi type="italic">which belonged</hi> to Judah, for Israel, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, <hi type="italic">even</hi> with the kings of Israel; and Zachariah his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen7397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7398" type="x-p"/> Here is an account of the reign of Jeroboam the second. I doubt it is an indication of the affection and adherence of the house of Jehu to the sins of <hi type="italic">Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin,</hi> that they called an heir-apparent to the crown by his name, thinking that an honourable name which in the book of God is infamous and stigmatized as much as any. <div eID="gen7398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7399" type="x-p"/> I. His reign was long, the longest of all the reigns of the kings of Israel: <hi type="italic">He reigned forty-one years;</hi> yet his contemporary Azariah, the king of Judah, reigned longer, even fifty-two years. This Jeroboam reigned just as long as Asa had done (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.10">1 Kings xv. 10</reference>), yet one did that which was good and the other that which was evil. We cannot measure men's characters by the length of their lives or by their outward prosperity. <hi type="italic">There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked.</hi> <div eID="gen7399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7400" type="x-p"/> II. His character was the same with that of the rest of those kings: <hi type="italic">He did that which was evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.24">v. 24</reference>), for <hi type="italic">he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam;</hi> he kept up the worship of the calves, and never left that, thinking there was no harm in it, because it had been the way of all his ancestors and predecessors. But a sin is never the less evil in God's sight, whatever it is in ours, for its being an ancient usage; and a frivolous plea it will be against doing good, that we have been accustomed to do evil. <div eID="gen7400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7401" type="x-p"/> III. Yet he prospered more than most of them, for though, in that one thing, he did evil in the sight of the Lord, yet it is likely, in other respects, there was some good found in him and therefore God owned him, 1. By prophecy. He raised up Jonah the son of Amittai, a Galilean (so much were those mistaken that said, <hi type="italic">Out of Galilee ariseth no prophet,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.52">John vii. 52</reference>), and by him intimated the purposes of his favour to Israel, notwithstanding their provocations, encouraged him and his kingdom to take up arms for the recovery of their ancient possessions, and (which would contribute not a little to their success) assured them of victory. It is a sign that God has not cast off his people if he continue faithful ministers among them; when Elisha, who strengthened the hands of Joash, was removed, Jonah was sent to encourage his son. Happy is the land that has a succession of prophets running parallel with a succession of princes, that the word of the Lord may endure for ever. Of this Jonah we read much in that little book of scripture that bears his name. It is probable that it was when he was a young man, and fit for such an expedition, that God sent him to Nineveh, and that it was when he had yet been but a little conversant with the visions of God that he flew off and fretted as he did; and, if so, this is an undoubted evidence of the forgiveness of his faults and follies, that he was afterwards employed as a messenger of mercy to Israel. A commission amounts to a pardon, and he that had himself found mercy, notwithstanding his provocations, could the better encourage them with the hope of mercy notwithstanding theirs. Some that have been foolish and passionate, and have gone about their work very awkwardly at first, yet afterwards have proved useful and eminent. Men must not be thrown away for every fault. 2. By providence. The event was <hi type="italic">according to the word of the Lord:</hi> his arms were successful; he <hi type="italic">restored the coast of Israel,</hi> recovered those frontier-towns and countries that lay from Hamath in the north to the sea of the plain, (that is, the sea of Sodom) in the south, all which the Syrians had possessed themselves of, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">v. 25</reference>. Two reasons are here given why God blessed them with those victories:—(1.) Because their distress was very great, which made them the objects of his compassion, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.26">v. 26</reference>. Though he saw not any signs of their repentance and formation, yet <hi type="italic">he saw their affliction, that it was very bitter.</hi> Those that lived in those countries which the enemies were masters of were miserably oppressed and enslaved, and could call nothing their own; the rest, we may suppose, were much impoverished by the frequent incursions the enemy made upon them to plunder them, and continually terrified by their threatenings, so that <hi type="italic">there was none shut up or left,</hi> both towns and countries were laid waste and stripped of their wealth, and no helper appeared. To this extremity were they reduced, in many parts of the country, in the beginning of Jeroboam's reign, when God, in mere pity to them, heard the cry of their affliction (for no mention is made here of the cry of their prayers), and wrought this deliverance for them by the hand of Jeroboam. Let those whose case is pitiable take comfort from the divine pity; we read of God's bowels of mercy (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa. lxiii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 20</reference>) and that he is full of compassion, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">Ps. lxxxvi. 15</reference>. (2.) Because the decree had not yet gone forth for their utter destruction; he had not as yet said <hi type="italic">he would blot out the name of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.27">v. 27</reference>), and because he had not said it he would not do it. If this be understood of the dispersion of the ten tribes, he did say it and do it, for that name still remains under heaven in the <hi type="italic">gospel Israel,</hi> and will to the end of time; and because they, at present, bore that name which was to have this lasting honour, he showed them this favour, as well as for the sake of the ancient honour of that name, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.23">ch. xiii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen7401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7402" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the conclusion of Jeroboam's reign. We read (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.28">v. 28</reference>) of his might, and how he warred, but (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.29">v. 29</reference>) he <hi type="italic">slept with his fathers;</hi> for the mightiest must yield to death, and there is no discharge in that war. Many prophets there had been in Israel, a constant succession of them in every age, but none of the prophets had left any of their prophecies in writing till those of this age began to do it, and their prophecies are part of the canon of scripture. It was in the reign of this Jeroboam that <hi type="italic">Hosea</hi> (who continued very long a prophet) began to prophesy, and he was the first that wrote his prophecies; therefore the word of the Lord by him is called <hi type="italic">the beginning of the word of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Hos. i. 2</reference>. Then <hi type="italic">that part of the word of the Lord</hi> began to be written. At the same time <hi type="italic">Amos</hi> prophesied, and wrote his prophecy, soon afterwards <hi type="italic">Micah,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">Isaiah,</hi> in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah. Thus God never left himself without witness, but, in the darkest and most degenerate ages of the church, raised up some to be burning and shining lights in it to their own age by their preaching and living, and a few by their writings to reflect light upon us on whom the ends of the world have come.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.14"/> <div eID="gen7402" type="x-p"/>

entries.a7e48c8026189aa70570094bbd33580734df4e44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3486"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <div sID="gen4920" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.6">2Ki 14:1-6</reference>. Amaziah's Good Reign over Judah.<div eID="gen4920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3486"/><hi type="bold">3-6. He did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, yet not like David his father--</hi>The beginning of his reign was excellent, for he acted the part of a constitutional king, according to the law of God, yet not with perfect sincerity of heart (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.2">2Ch 25:2</reference>). As in the case of his father Joash, the early promise was belied by the devious course he personally followed in later life (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14">2Ch 20:14</reference>), as well as by the public irregularities he tolerated in the kingdom. <div eID="gen4921" type="x-p"/>
entries.42f6ed8233963f3e82cf2dda212eb4e1b0a38df0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3489"/><div sID="gen4925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3489"/><hi type="bold">7. He slew of Edom in the valley of salt ten thousand--</hi>In the reign of Joram the Edomites had revolted (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.20">2Ki 8:20</reference>). But Amaziah, determined to reduce them to their former subjection, formed a hostile expedition against them, in which he routed their army and made himself master of their capital.<div eID="gen4925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the valley of salt--</hi>that part of the Ghor which comprises the salt and sandy plain to the south of the Dead Sea.<div eID="gen4926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Selah--</hi>literally, "the rock"; generally thought to be Petra.<div eID="gen4927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joktheel--</hi>that is, "given" or "conquered by God." See the history of this conquest more fully detailed (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.6-2Chr.25.16">2Ch 25:6-16</reference>).<div eID="gen4928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4929" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8-2Kgs.14.16">2Ki 14:8-16</reference>. Joash Defeats Him. <div eID="gen4929" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d3abc5b0392e97f44028b25e8d9f9a52c40aa16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3490"/><div sID="gen4930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3490"/><hi type="bold">8. Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash, the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel--</hi>This bold and haughty challenge, which was most probably stimulated by a desire of satisfaction for the outrages perpetrated by the discharged auxiliaries of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Ch 25:13</reference>) on the towns that lay in their way home, as well as by revenge for the massacre of his ancestors by Jehu (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.1-2Kgs.9.37">2Ki 9:1-37</reference>) sprang, there is little doubt, from pride and self-confidence, inspired by his victory over the Edomites. <div eID="gen4930" type="x-p"/>
entries.f518299ea6933b2fa5d1ba0f20229f5246ce5647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3491"/><div sID="gen4931" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3491"/><hi type="bold">9. Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah--</hi>People in the East very often express their sentiments in a parabolic form, especially when they intend to convey unwelcome truths or a contemptuous sneer. This was the design of the admonitory fable related by Joash in his reply. The thistle, a low shrub, might be chosen to represent Amaziah, a petty prince; the cedar, the powerful sovereign of Israel, and the wild beast that trampled down the thistle the overwhelming army with which Israel could desolate Judah. But, perhaps, without making so minute an application, the parable may be explained generally, as describing in a striking manner the effects of pride and ambition, towering far beyond their natural sphere, and sure to fall with a sudden and ruinous crash. The moral of the fable is contained in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.10">2Ki 14:10</reference>. <div eID="gen4931" type="x-p"/>
entries.07708f5101264573f6a8190ae89428abc304ed61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3492"/><div sID="gen4932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3492"/><hi type="bold">11-14. But Amaziah would not hear--</hi>The sarcastic tenor of this reply incited the king of Judah the more; for, being in a state of judicial blindness and infatuation (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20">2Ch 25:20</reference>), he was immovably determined on war. But the superior energy of Joash surprised him ere he had completed his military preparations. Pouring a large army into the territory of Judah, he encountered Amaziah in a pitched battle, routed his army, and took him prisoner. Then having marched to Jerusalem [2Ki 14:13], he not only demolished part of the city walls, but plundered the treasures of the palace and temple. Taking hostages to prevent any further molestation from Judah, he terminated the war. Without leaving a garrison in Jerusalem, he returned to his capital with all convenient speed, his presence and all his forces being required to repel the troublesome incursions of the Syrians.<div eID="gen4932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4933" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.17-2Kgs.14.20">2Ki 14:17-20</reference>. He Is Slain by a Conspiracy. <div eID="gen4933" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ccc921c64cb3b93b5ed106b971114e389dd4084: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3493"/><div sID="gen4934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3493"/><hi type="bold">19-20. they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem--</hi>Amaziah's apostasy (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.27">2Ch 25:27</reference>) was followed by a general maladministration, especially the disastrous issue of the war with Israel. The ruinous condition of Jerusalem, the plunder of the temple, and the loss of their children who were taken as hostages [2Ki 14:13, 14], lost him the respect and attachment not of the grandees only, but of his subjects generally, who were in rebellion. The king fled in terror to Lachish, a frontier town of the Philistines, where, however, he was traced and murdered. His friends had his corpse brought without any pomp or ceremony, in a chariot to Jerusalem, where he was interred among his royal ancestors.<div eID="gen4934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4935" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.21">2Ki 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.22">22</reference>. Azariah Succeeds Him. <div eID="gen4935" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e9c3d9555ecf228fd5e3daa91d541743974f44f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3494"/><div sID="gen4936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3494"/><hi type="bold">21. all the people of Judah took Azariah--</hi>or Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.30">2Ki 15:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.1">2Ch 26:1</reference>). The popular opposition had been personally directed against Amaziah as the author of their calamities, but it was not extended to his family or heir. <div eID="gen4936" type="x-p"/>
entries.599fc4c7c357861fef59095c82c951c0cadac6fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3495"/><div sID="gen4937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3495"/><hi type="bold">22. He built Elath--</hi>fortified that seaport. It had revolted with the rest of Edom, but was now recovered by Uzziah. His father, who did not complete the conquest of Edom, had left him that work to do.<div eID="gen4937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4938" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.23-2Kgs.14.29">2Ki 14:23-29</reference>. Jeroboam's Wicked Reign over Israel. <div eID="gen4938" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbaf61fb24be29ee9742517d012a8bd881242997: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3496"/><div sID="gen4939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3496"/><hi type="bold">23. Jeroboam, the son of Joash king of Israel--</hi>This was Jeroboam II who, on regaining the lost territory, raised the kingdom to great political power (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>), but adhered to the favorite religious policy of the Israelitish sovereigns (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.24">2Ki 14:24</reference>). While God granted him so great a measure of national prosperity and eminence, the reason is expressly stated (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.26">2Ki 14:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.27">27</reference>) to be that the purposes of the divine covenant forbade as yet the overthrow of the kingdom of the ten tribes (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.23">2Ki 13:23</reference>). <chapter eID="2Kgs.14"/>

entries.12ece3b78a261facfef2b8f3ad85f8907779f9e5: <div eID="gen12896" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen12897" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> Amaziah begins to reign well; his victory over the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.7">2Kgs 14:1-7</reference>. He challenges Jehoash, king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.8">2Kgs 14:8</reference>. Jehoash's parable of the thistle and the cedar, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.9">2Kgs 14:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.10">2Kgs 14:10</reference>. The two armies meet at Beth-shemesh; and the men of Judah are defeated, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.11">2Kgs 14:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.12">2Kgs 14:12</reference>. Jehoash takes Jerusalem, breaks down four hundred cubits of the wall; takes the treasures of the king's house, and of the temple; and takes hostages, and returns to Samaria, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.13">2Kgs 14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.14">2Kgs 14:14</reference>. The death and burial of both these kings, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.20">2Kgs 14:15-20</reference>. Azariah, the son of Amaziah, made king; he builds Elath, vv. 21, 22. Jeroboam the second is made king over Israel: his wicked reign and death, vv. 23-29. <div eID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12897" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12899" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen12899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12900" type="x-p"/> In the second year of Joash - This second year should be understood as referring to the time when his father Jehoahaz associated him with himself in the kingdom: for he reigned two years with his father; so this second year of Joash is the first of his absolute and independent government. - See Calmet.
entries.7b4e0813312759200d4d0f95523ce3b00a55c166: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen12900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12901" type="x-p"/> As soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand - No doubt those wicked men, Jozachar and Jehozabad, who murdered his father, had considerable power and influence; and therefore he found it dangerous to bring them to justice, till he was assured of the loyalty of his other officers: when this was clear, he called them to account, and put them to death.
entries.524a02b1603956c07dfffdb2d2cf844ba6b07069: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen12901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12902" type="x-p"/> But the children of the murderers he slew not - Here he showed his conscientious regard for the law of Moses; for God had positively said, The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin, <reference osisRef="Deu.24.16">Deu 24:16</reference>.
entries.a90d732bc70a6b2ff17745518084c72e587570da: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen12902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> He slew of Edom to the valley of salt - This war is more circumstantially related in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.5">2Chr 25:5</reference>, etc. The Idumeans had arisen in the reign of Joram king of Judah, and shaken off the yoke of the house of David. Amaziah determined to reduce them to obedience; he therefore levied an army of three hundred thousand men in his own kingdom, and hired a hundred thousand Israelites, at the price of one hundred talents. When he was about to depart at the head of this numerous army, a prophet came to him and ordered him to dismiss the Israelitish army, for God was not with them: and on the king of Judah expressing regret for the loss of his hundred talents, he was answered, that the Lord could give him much more than that. He obeyed, sent back the Israelites, and at the head of his own men attacked the Edomites in the valley of salt, slew ten thousand on the spot, and took ten thousand prisoners, all of whom he precipitated from the rock, or Selah, which was afterwards called Joktheel, a place or city supposed to be the same with Petra, which gave name to Arabia Petraea, where there must have been a great precipice, from which the place took its name of Selah or Petra.
entries.dffc689d0437ea1a9141f74bc053b8439b5afcea: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12904" type="x-p"/> Come, let us look one another in the face - This was a real declaration of war; and the ground of it is most evident from this circumstance: that the one hundred thousand men of Israel that had been dismissed, though they had the stipulated money, taking the advantage of Amaziah's absence, fell upon the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and smote three thousand men, and took much spoil, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.10-2Chr.25.13">2Chr 25:10-13</reference>. Amaziah no doubt remonstrated with Jehoash, but to no purpose; and therefore he declared war against him.
entries.6283d4518f057bdb4925cbc1d6611ad45901e67a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen12904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> Jehoash - sent to Amaziah - saying - The meaning of this parable is plain. The thistle that was in Lebanon - Amaziah, king of Judah, sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon - Jehoash, king of Israel, saying, Give thy daughter - a part of thy kingdom, to my son to wife - to be united to, and possessed by the kings of Judah. And there passed by a wild beast - Jehoash and his enraged army, and trode down the thistle - utterly discomfited Amaziah and his troops, pillaged the temple, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem: see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.12-2Kgs.14.14">2Kgs 14:12-14</reference>. Probably Amaziah had required certain cities of Israel to be given up to Judah; if so, this accounts for that part of the parable, Give thy daughter to my son to wife.
entries.48e643a4ac207d5a6eb10e623093abd530091f14: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> Glory of this, and tarry at home - There is a vast deal of insolent dignity in this remonstrance of Jehoash: but it has nothing conciliatory; no proposal of making amends for the injury his army had done to the unoffending inhabitants of Judah. The ravages committed by the army of Jehoash were totally unprovoked, and they were base and cowardly; they fell upon women, old men, and children, and butchered them in cold blood, for all the effective men were gone off with their king against the Edomites. The quarrel of Amaziah was certainly just, yet he was put to the rout; he did meddle to his hurt; he fell, and Judah fell with him, as Jehoash had said: but why was this? Why it came of God; for he had brought the gods of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burnt incense to them; therefore God delivered them into the hands of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.14">2Chr 25:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.20">2Chr 25:20</reference>. This was the reason why the Israelites triumphed.
entries.65014ebecfe58c1b744267c6dfa7ab396ff9a728: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12907" type="x-p"/> Took Amaziah king of Judah - It is plain that Amaziah afterwards had his liberty; but how or on what terms he got it, is not known. See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.14">2Kgs 14:14</reference> (note).
entries.9778e354c00a61f98932d99b88206d6a6a92eaa3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen12907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12908" type="x-p"/> And he took - hostages - התערבות hattaaruboth, pledges; from ערב arab, to pledge, give security, etc., for the performance of some promise. See the meaning of this word interpreted in the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.38.17">Gen 38:17</reference> (note). It is likely that Amaziah gave some of the nobles or some of his own family as hostages, that he might regain his liberty; and they were to get their liberty when he had fulfilled his engagements; but of what kind these were we cannot tell, nor, indeed, how he got his liberty.
entries.fa27b4d8b9c0078cec5f26c8b5aacb78f2280fa8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen12908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12909" type="x-p"/> How he fought with Amaziah - The only fighting between them was the battle already mentioned; and this is minutely related in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.21-2Chr.25.24">2Chr 25:21-24</reference>.
entries.7e0bf05dbc30ad10d4521e6c9dc3ba4d00a9941d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen12909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12910" type="x-p"/> They made a conspiracy against him - His defeat by Jehoash, and the consequent pillaging of the temple, and emptying the royal exchequer, and the dismantling of Jerusalem, had made him exceedingly unpopular; so that probably the whole of the last fifteen years of his life were a series of troubles and distresses.
entries.2482b2cfa5405a7569c9c1602a5eb66c6c558cec: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen12910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12911" type="x-p"/> Took Azariah - He is also called Uzziah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.1">2Chr 26:1</reference>. The former signifies, The help of the Lord; the latter, The strength of the Lord.
entries.5f2cbc71981b9b3a04eaffa262f5e809cd96a7bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen12911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12912" type="x-p"/> He built Elath - This city belonged to the Edomites; and was situated on the eastern branch of the Red Sea, thence called the Elanitic Gulf. It had probably suffered much in the late war; and was now rebuilt by Uzziah, and brought entirely under the dominion of Judah.
entries.0bb38cee3ca245a8321b79aafdb7eeaa4975b576: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen12912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12913" type="x-p"/> He restored the coast of Israel - From the description that is here given, it appears that Jeroboam reconquered all the territory that had been taken from the kings of Israel; so that Jeroboam the second left the kingdom as ample as it was when the ten tribes separated under Jeroboam the first.
entries.c5bd3e2dffb6c85b54c4ef3104d484115a2040b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen12913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12914" type="x-p"/> The Lord saw the affliction of Israel - It appears that about this time Israel had been greatly reduced; and great calamities had fallen upon all indiscriminately; even the diseased and captives in the dungeon had the hand of God heavy upon them, and there was no helper; and then God sent Jonah to encourage them, and to assure them of better days. He was the first of the prophets, after Samuel, whose writings are preserved; yet the prophecy delivered on this occasion is not extant; for what is now in the prophecies of Jonah, relates wholly to Nineveh.
entries.5f18e28bda80fc7e07b699b90a4a46f7eda74a0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen12914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12915" type="x-p"/> How he warred, and - recovered Damascus - We learn from <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3-1Chr.18.11">1Chr 18:3-11</reference>, that David had conquered all Syria, and put garrisons in Damascus and other places, and laid all the Syrians under tribute; but this yoke they had not only shaken off, but they had conquered a considerable portion of the Israelitish territory, and added it to Syria. These latter Jeroboam now recovered; and thus the places which anciently belonged to Judah by David's conquests, and were repossessed by Syria, he now conquered, and added to Israel.
entries.8f5e60d1b519995defa1f2b164d41f1ae224b977: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen12915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12916" type="x-p"/> Jeroboam slept with his fathers - He died a natural death; and was regularly succeeded by his son Zachariah, who, reigning badly, was, after six months, slain by Shallum, who succeeded him, and reigned but one month, being slain by Menahem, who succeeded him, and reigned ten years over Israel. Amos the prophet lived in the reign of Jeroboam; and was accused by Amaziah, one of the idolatrous priests of Beth-el, of having predicted the death of Jeroboam by the sword, but this was a slander: what he did predict, and which came afterwards to pass, may be seen <reference osisRef="Amo.7.10-Amo.7.17">Amo 7:10-17</reference>. The interregnum referred to in the margin cannot be accounted for in a satisfactory manner.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.14"/> <div eID="gen12916" type="x-p"/>

entries.a510f924e0ef3f8c573177726759948d2b919d58: <div eID="gen5309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5310" type="x-p"/> Reign of Amaziah of Judah (cf. 2 Chron 25). - 2Ki 14:1-7. Length and spirit of his reign, and his victory over the Edomites. - 2Ki 14:1. Amaziah began to reign in the second year of Joash of Israel. Now as Joash of Israel ascended the throne, according to 2Ki 13:10, in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah, the latter cannot have reigned thirty-nine full years, which might be reckoned as forty (2Ki 12:1), according to the principle of reckoning the current years as complete years, if the commencement of his reign took place a month or two before Nisan, and his death occurred a month or two after, without its being necessary to assume a regency.
entries.4f017042d88e16d49ccbd612df25cfbab1d737ad: 2Ki 14:2-4 <div eID="gen5310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5311" type="x-p"/> Amaziah reigned twenty-nine years in the same theocratical spirit as his father Joash, only not like his ancestor David, i.e., according to the correct explanation in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.2">2Ch 25:2</reference>, not with שׁלם לבב (see at 1Ki 11:4), since Amaziah, like his father Joash (see at 2Ki 12:3), fell into idolatry in the closing years of his reign (cf. 2Ch 25:14.). - Only the high places were not taken away, etc.
entries.08cbb240c0e2a21551c3813c5a201bc9fa4a4b28: 2Ki 14:5-6 <div eID="gen5311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5312" type="x-p"/> After establishing his own government, he punished the murderers of his father with death; but, according to the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.16">Deu 24:16</reference>, he did not slay their children also, as was commonly the custom in the East in ancient times, and may very frequently have been done in Israel as well. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> ימוּת is correct, and the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ימת is an unnecessary alteration made after Deuteronomy.
entries.93091379d6394d0b59c603f45a15f4184bc8e191: 2Ki 14:7 <div eID="gen5312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5313" type="x-p"/> The brief account of the defeat of the Edomites in the Salt Valley and of the taking of the city of Sela is completed by <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.6">2Ch 25:6</reference>-16. According to the latter, Amaziah sought to strengthen his own considerable army by the addition of 100,000 Israelitish mercenaries; but at the exhortation of a prophet he sent the hired Israelites away again, at which they were so enraged, that on their way home they plundered several of the cities of Judah and put many men to death. The Edomites had revolted from Judah in the reign of Joram (2Ki 8:20.); Amaziah now sought to re-establish his rule over them, in which he was so far successful, that he completely defeated them, slaying 10,000 in the battle and then taking their capital, so that his successor Uzziah was also able to incorporate the Edomitish port of Elath in his own kingdom once more (2Ki 14:22). On the Salt Valley (גּי־המּלח for גּיא־המּלח in the Chronicles), a marshy salt plain in the south of the Dead Sea, see at 2Sa 8:13. According to <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:12</reference> of the Chronicles, in addition to the 10,000 who were slain in battle, 10,000 Edomites were taken prisoners and cast headlong alive from the top of a rock. הסּלע (<hi type="italic">the</hi> rock) with the article, because the epithet is founded upon the peculiar nature of the city, was probably the capital of the Edomites, called by the Greeks ἡ Πέτρα, and bore this name from its situation and the mode in which it was built, since it was erected in a valley surrounded by rocks, and that in such a manner that the houses were partly hewn in the natural rock. Of this commercial city, which was still flourishing in the first centuries of the Christian era, splendid ruins have been preserved in a valley on the eastern side of the ghor which runs down to the Elanitic Gulf, about two days’ journey from the southern extremity of the Dead Sea, on the east of Mount Hor, to which the Crusaders gave the name of vallis Moysi, and which the Arabs still call Wady Musa (see Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. pp. 512ff., and for the history of this city, pp. 574ff., and Ritter’s Erdkunde, xiv. pp. 1103ff.).
entries.15e1a157fbb2134afeeea5c80e9f59412dec2391: 2Ki 14:8-14 <div eID="gen5313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5314" type="x-p"/> War with Joash of Israel. - 2Ki 14:8. Amaziah then sent a challenge to the Israelitish king Joash to go to war with him. The outward reason for this was no doubt the hostile acts that had been performed by the Israelitish troops, which had been hired for the war with Edom and then sent back again (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Ch 25:13</reference>). But the inward ground was the pride which had crept upon Amaziah in consequence of his victory over the Edomites, and had so far carried him away, that he not only forgot the Lord his God, to whom he was indebted for this victory, and brought to Jerusalem the gods of the Edomites which he had taken in the war and worshipped them, and silenced with threats the prophet who condemned this idolatry (2Ch 25:14.), but in his proud reliance upon his own power challenged the Israelitish king to war.
entries.45624062653c84cd6f1e1b04f597c33d25702852: 2Ki 14:15-17 <div eID="gen5317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5318" type="x-p"/> The repetition of the notice concerning the end of the reign of Joash, together with the formula from 2Ki 13:12 and 2Ki 13:13, may probably be explained from the fact, that in the annals of the kings of Israel it stood after the account of the war between Jehoash and Amaziah. This may be inferred from the circumstance that the name of Joash is spelt invariably יהואשׁ here, whereas in the closing notices in 2Ki 13:12 and 2Ki 13:13 we have the later form יואשׁ, the one which was no doubt adopted by the author of our books. But he might be induced to give these notices once more as he found them in his original sources, from the statement in 2Ki 14:17, that Amaziah outlived Jehoash fifteen years, seeing therein a manifestation of the grace of God, who would not destroy Amaziah notwithstanding his pride, but delivered him, through the death of his victor, from further injuries at his hands. As Amaziah ascended the throne in the second year of the sixteen years’ reign of Jehoash, and before his war with Israel made war upon the Edomites and overcame them, the war with Israel can only fall in the closing years of Jehoash, and this king cannot very long have survived his triumph over the king of Judah.
entries.78793771cd07729ba2ef9fe088d25a79a08577d2: 2Ki 14:18-19 <div eID="gen5318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5319" type="x-p"/> Conspiracy against Amaziah. - 2Ki 14:19. Amaziah, like his father Joash, did not die a natural death. They made a conspiracy against him at Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish, whither murderers were sent after him, who slew him there. The earlier commentators sought for the cause of this conspiracy in the unfortunate result of the war with Jehoash; but this conjecture is at variance with the circumstance that the conspiracy did not break out till fifteen years or more after that event. It is true that in <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.27">2Ch 25:27</reference> we read “from the time that Amaziah departed from the Lord, they formed a conspiracy against him;” but even this statement cannot be understood in any other way than that Amaziah’s apostasy gave occasion for discontent, which eventually led to a conspiracy. For his apostasy began with the introduction of Edomitish deities into Jerusalem after the defeat of the Edomites, and therefore before the war with Jehoash, in the first part of his reign, whereas the conspiracy cannot possibly have lasted fifteen years or more before it came to a head. Lachish, in the lowlands of Judah, has probably been preserved in the ruins of Um Lakis (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference>).
entries.a5086871698ab95a32c5d50eb1e184a62643e196: 2Ki 14:20 “They lifted him upon the horses,” i.e., upon the hearse to which the king’s horses had been harnessed, and brought him to Jerusalem, where he was buried with his fathers, i.e., in the royal tomb.
entries.9d5c435db10ff3cc61a6fdda189d9edf8ccb8bf6: 2Ki 14:21 <div eID="gen5319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5320" type="x-p"/> All the people of Judah, i.e., the whole nation, not the whole of the men of war (Thenius), thereupon made his son Azariah (Uzziah) king, who was only sixteen years old. עזריה or עזריהוּ is the name given to this king here and 2Ki 15:1, 2Ki 15:6,2Ki 15:8, 2Ki 15:17, 2Ki 15:23, and 2Ki 15:27, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.12">1Ch 3:12</reference>; whereas in 2Ki 15:13, 2Ki 15:30, 2Ki 15:32, 2Ki 15:34; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.1">2Ch 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.3">2Ch 26:3</reference>,<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.11">2Ch 26:11</reference>, etc., and also <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>; Hos 1:1; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Amo 1:1</reference>, and Zec 14:5, he is called עזּיה or עזּיּהוּ (Uzziah). This variation in the name is too constant to be attributable to a copyist’s error. Even the conjecture that Azariah adopted the name Uzziah as king, or that it was given to him by the soldiers after a successful campaign (Thenius), does not explain the use of the two names in our historical books. We must rather assume that the two names, which are related in meaning, were used promiscuously. עזריה signifies “in Jehovah is help;” עזּיה, “whose strength is Jehovah.” This is favoured by the circumstance adduced by Bertheau, that among the descendants of Kohath we also find an Uzziah who bears the name Azariah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.9">1Ch 6:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.21">1Ch 6:21</reference>), and similarly among the descendants of Heman an Uzziel with the name Azarel (<reference osisRef="1Chr.25.4">1Ch 25:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.18">1Ch 25:18</reference>).
entries.d191af8c2aad392efcced31b2235885954083fc1: 2Ki 14:22 <div eID="gen5320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5321" type="x-p"/> Immediately after his ascent of the throne, Uzziah built, i.e., fortified, Elath, the Idumaean port (see at 1Ki 9:26), and restored it to Judah again. It is evident from this that Uzziah completed the renewed subjugation of Edom which his father had begun. The position in which this notice stands, immediately after his ascent of the throne and before the account of the duration and character of his reign, may be explained in all probability from the importance of the work itself, which not only distinguished the commencement of his reign, but also gave evident of its power.
entries.2c92b45db8a4d79f7dabee09dc885ffb6c5375ea: 2Ki 14:23-24 <div eID="gen5321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5322" type="x-p"/> Reign of Jeroboam II of Israel. - 2Ki 14:23. The statement that Jeroboam the son of Joash (Jehoash) ascended the throne in the fifteenth year of Amaziah, agrees with 2Ki 14:17, according to which Amaziah outlived Jehoash fifteen years, since Amaziah reigned twenty-nine years. On the other hand, the forty-one years’ duration of his reign does not agree with the statement in 2Ki 15:8, that his son Zachariah did not become king till the thirty-eighth year of Azariah (Uzziah); and therefore Thenius proposes to alter the number 41 into 51, Ewald into 53. For further remarks, see 2Ki 15:8. Jeroboam also adhered firmly to the image-worship of his ancestors, but he raised his kingdom again to great power.
entries.bb1428923ec227c7a23c6db8bb97e589dae3f57c: 2Ki 14:25 <div eID="gen5322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5323" type="x-p"/> He brought back (השׁיב), i.e., restored, the boundary of Israel from towards Hamath in the north, to the point to which the kingdom extended in the time of Solomon (1Ki 8:65), to the sea of the Arabah (the present Ghor), i.e., to the Dead Sea (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">Deu 3:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.4.49">Deu 4:49</reference>, from which this designation of the southern border of the kingdom of the ten tribes arose), “according to the word of the Lord, which He had spoken through the prophet Jonah,” who had probably used this designation of the southern boundary, which was borrowed from the Pentateuch, in the announcement which he made. The extent of the kingdom of Israel in the reign of Jeroboam is defined in the same manner in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>, but instead of הערבה ים the הערבה נחל is mentioned, i.e., in all probability the Wady el Ashy, which formed the boundary between Moab and Edom; from which we may see that Jeroboam had also subjugated the Moabites to his kingdom, which is not only rendered probable by 2Ki 3:6., but is also implied in the words that he restored the former boundary of the kingdom of Israel-On the prophet Jonah, the son of Amittai, see the Comm. on Jon 1:1. Gath-hepher, in the tribe of Zebulun, is the present village of Meshed, to the north of Nazareth (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.13">Jos 19:13</reference>).
entries.027ec99bb812daa5af8aef600f414cd8567fb179: 2Ki 14:26-27 <div eID="gen5323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5324" type="x-p"/> The higher ground for this strengthening of Israel in the time of Jeroboam was to be found in the compassion of God. The Lord saw the great oppression and helpless condition of Israel, and had not yet pronounced the decree of rejection. He therefore sent help through Jeroboam. מאד מרה without the article, and governed by ישׂ אני (see Ewald, §293, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), signifies very bitter, מרה having taken the meaning of מרר. This is the explanation adopted in all the ancient versions, and also by Dietrich in Ges. Lex. וגו עצוּר ואפס, verbatim from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference>, to show that the kingdom of Israel had been brought to the utmost extremity of distress predicted there by Moses, and it was necessary that the Lord should interpose with His help, if His people were not utterly to perish. דבּר לא: He had not yet spoken, i.e., had not yet uttered the decree of rejection through the mouth of a prophet. To blot out the name under the heavens is an abbreviated expression for: among the nations who dwelt under the heavens.
entries.4e0a43a1581b34428bad9d1d35f827d306d4f695: 2Ki 14:28 <div eID="gen5324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5325" type="x-p"/> Of the rest of the history of Jeroboam we have nothing more than an intimation that he brought back Damascus and Hamath of Judah to Israel, i.e., subjugated it again to the kingdom of Israel. ליהוּדה is a periphrastic form for the genitive, as proper names do not admit of any form of the construct state, and in this case the simple genitive would not have answered so well to the fact. For the meaning is: “whatever in the two kingdoms of Damascus and Hamath had formerly belonged to Judah in the times of David and Solomon.” By Damascus and Hamath we are not to understand the cities, but the kingdoms; for not only did the city of Hamath never belong to the kingdom of Israel, but it was situated outside the boundaries laid down by Moses for Israel (see at Num 34:8). It cannot, therefore, have been re-conquered (השׁיב) by Jeroboam. It was different with the city of Damascus, which David had conquered and even Solomon had not permanently lost (see at 1Ki 11:24). Consequently in the case of Damascus the capital is included in the kingdom.
entries.a7266ce26e0be5433d91d2106f5f913c67363e28: 2Ki 14:29 <div eID="gen5325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5326" type="x-p"/> As Jeroboam reigned forty-one years, his death occurred in the twenty-seventh year of Uzziah. If, then, his son did not begin to reign till the thirty-eight year of Uzziah, as is stated in 2Ki 15:8, he cannot have come to the throne immediately after his father’s death (see at 2Ki 15:8).  <chapter eID="2Kgs.14"/> <div eID="gen5326" type="x-p"/>
